Free and open source milestones.GNU Project announced: Richard Stallman announced a free Unix-like system, and GNU is a recursive joke that stands for GNU's Not Unix.
Free and open source milestones.Free Software Foundation: Founded by Stallman to promote and fund the free software movement, it champions users' freedom to run, study and share code.
Free and open source milestones.GPL license: It is a copyleft license, which requires anyone sharing a modified version to share it under the same freedoms.
Free and open source milestones.Linux kernel: A Finnish student, Linus Torvalds, announced it online as just a hobby, and it now runs most servers and every Android phone.
Free and open source milestones.Debian: Founded by Ian Murdock, the name combines Debra, his then-girlfriend, and his own name, Ian.
Free and open source milestones.Apache web server: Its name is often joked to mean a patchy server, and it powered a large share of the early web.
Free and open source milestones.Term open source coined: Coined at a meeting in California after Netscape released its browser code, as a friendlier name than free software.
Free and open source milestones.Creative Commons: Cofounded by law professor Lawrence Lessig, it gave creators easy licenses to share their work with chosen rights.
Free and open source milestones.Ubuntu: The name is a Zulu and Xhosa word often glossed as humanity toward others, chosen by founder Mark Shuttleworth.
Free and open source milestones.Android open-sourced: Google released the mobile platform with the Open Handset Alliance, and the first phone, the T-Mobile G1, arrived that year.

Mixed-unit temperatures: which is hotter.0 K: Absolute zero is where particle motion is at its minimum; scientists have cooled atoms to billionths of a degree above it but never reached it.
Mixed-unit temperatures: which is hotter.-40 °F: It is the one temperature where the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales give the same number.
Mixed-unit temperatures: which is hotter.0 °F: Fahrenheit set his zero at the temperature of a freezing mix of ice, water and salt, the coldest he could easily make.
Mixed-unit temperatures: which is hotter.32 °F: On this scale water freezes at pure sea-level pressure, and it looks odd because Fahrenheit built his scale around brine and body heat.
Mixed-unit temperatures: which is hotter.300 K: It's roughly a warm room, and the Kelvin scale uses no degree sign because it is measured from absolute zero.
Mixed-unit temperatures: which is hotter.100 °F: Normal body temperature is about 98.6 °F, and doctors generally call 100.4 °F a fever, so this would be a high fever.
Mixed-unit temperatures: which is hotter.212 °F: At altitude water boils below this point, around 95 °C (203 °F) in Denver, and pressure cookers push it higher.
Mixed-unit temperatures: which is hotter.400 K: The sunlit lunar surface reaches roughly this temperature at midday, hotter than boiling water, while night plunges below -170 °C.
Mixed-unit temperatures: which is hotter.451 °F: This is the figure in the title of Bradbury's novel, said to be the temperature at which book paper catches fire.
Mixed-unit temperatures: which is hotter.1,000 K: At this heat metal glows a clear red-orange, since objects start to give off visible light somewhere around 800 K.

Roots and constants by value.Cube root of 8: Because 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, it is a perfect cube; the ancient Greek puzzle of doubling a cube's volume needs the cube root of 2.
Roots and constants by value.Square root of 5: It is tied to the golden ratio, which equals (1 + the root of 5) / 2, about 1.618.
Roots and constants by value.e: Jacob Bernoulli bumped into it while studying compound interest; it is irrational, with digits that never repeat.
Roots and constants by value.Cube root of 27: A 3 x 3 x 3 block holds 27 small cubes; a Rubik's Cube mimics that, though its core is really a hidden mechanism.
Roots and constants by value.π: Babylonians used 3.125 for it, and Archimedes trapped it between 3 1/7 and 3 10/71 using polygons.
Roots and constants by value.Square root of 10: Chinese mathematician Zhang Heng used this root as an approximation of pi, since the two are close.
Roots and constants by value.Cube root of 100: A cube with a volume of 100 cubic centimetres would have edges just under 4.65 cm long.
Roots and constants by value.Square root of 30: It lies between 5 and 6 because 30 sits between 25 and 36; the Babylonian method homes in on it by repeated averaging.
Roots and constants by value.Square root of 99: Since 99 is one less than 100, its root falls just shy of 10, by roughly 0.05.
Roots and constants by value.Cube root of 1,000: A litre fills a cube 10 cm on each side, since 1,000 cubic centimetres have a cube root of 10.

When these national constitutions were a.United States: It is the world's oldest written national constitution still in force.
When these national constitutions were a.Poland's May Constitution: Often called Europe's first modern written constitution, it was cut short by the partitions of Poland.
When these national constitutions were a.Norway: Adopted on 17 May at Eidsvoll, and Norway celebrates that day as Constitution Day.
When these national constitutions were a.Belgium: Written after independence from the Netherlands in 1830, it became a liberal model for Europe.
When these national constitutions were a.Meiji Japan: Granted by the emperor, it created the Imperial Diet.
When these national constitutions were a.Mexico: Born from revolution, it is famous for its labour and land reform provisions.
When these national constitutions were a.Weimar Germany: It gave women the vote, and its Article 48 emergency powers eventually helped Hitler.
When these national constitutions were a.Ireland: Bunreacht na hEireann replaced the Free State constitution and was approved by referendum.
When these national constitutions were a.India: It is the world's longest written national constitution; Ambedkar chaired its drafting committee.
When these national constitutions were a.Spain: Approved after Franco's death, it restored democracy and the monarchy.

Standard things by length.Credit card: ISO 7810 ID-1 is the size shared by driving licences and many ID cards, so that one wallet slot fits them all.
Standard things by length.US banknote: All US bills are the same size, unlike in many countries, and they are made of cotton and linen, not paper.
Standard things by length.Unsharpened pencil: According to a popular estimate, a single pencil can draw a line about 56 km long before it wears down.
Standard things by length.Long side of A4 paper: A4 is based on a ratio of the square root of 2, so folding it in half keeps the same proportions.
Standard things by length.Baseball bat (max): Major League rules cap the length of a bat at 42 inches, which is 1.07 m, and its diameter at 2.61 inches.
Standard things by length.Standard US door height: Doors are typically 6 feet 8 inches tall, or 2.03 m, which is why very tall people may bump their heads in old houses.
Standard things by length.Ping pong table: A regulation table is nine feet long, or 2.74 m, and its net is 15.25 cm high.
Standard things by length.Small shipping container: The 20-foot container is the origin of TEU, a standard unit used to measure shipping cargo.
Standard things by length.Bowling lane: A bowling lane is 60 feet from the foul line to the head pin, and its pins are 15 inches tall.
Standard things by length.Tennis court: A tennis court is 78 feet long, and the length is the same for singles and doubles.

Fill in the famous number.Chanel No. ___ perfume: Coco Chanel picked the fifth sample vial, saying 5 was her lucky number, and it became one of the world's best-selling scents.
Fill in the famous number.___-Eleven stores: The convenience store chain was named for its original hours, 7 am to 11 pm, which at the time were considered shockingly long.
Fill in the famous number.Apollo ___, first on the Moon: This was the mission on which Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed in July 1969, and Michael Collins stayed in orbit.
Fill in the famous number.WD-___ spray: The 'WD' stands for Water Displacement, and 40 is the number of the formula the chemists finally got right, in 1953, for the aerospace industry.
Fill in the famous number.Area ___ (Nevada): The government did not publicly acknowledge this Nevada air base until 2013, which helped fuel decades of UFO lore.
Fill in the famous number.Studio ___ nightclub: New York's famous disco on West 54th Street was owned by Steve Rubell and Ian Schrager, and its guests included Warhol and Jagger.
Fill in the famous number.Heinz ___ Varieties: Henry Heinz's '57' was invented for the slogan; he had more than 57 products by then, but he liked the sound of the number.
Fill in the famous number.Route ___: This highway from Chicago to Santa Monica was nicknamed the Mother Road by John Steinbeck, and a 1946 song told drivers to 'get your kicks' on it.
Fill in the famous number.Levi's ___ jeans: Levi's riveted jeans got the 501 lot number in the 1890s, and today's button-fly pair still looks much like the original working pants.
Fill in the famous number.Boeing ___ jumbo jet: The world's first wide-body airliner flew in 1969, and its upper-deck hump let the cockpit sit above a cargo door that swings open in the nose.

The Beatles' UK studio albums, in order.Please Please Me: The Beatles recorded almost all of it in a single day in February 1963, in about ten hours.
The Beatles' UK studio albums, in order.A Hard Day's Night: It was the first Beatles album made up entirely of Lennon and McCartney originals.
The Beatles' UK studio albums, in order.Beatles for Sale: It had covers of Chuck Berry and Carl Perkins, and a cover photo showing the band looking weary.
The Beatles' UK studio albums, in order.Help!: It contains Yesterday, one of the most covered songs in history.
The Beatles' UK studio albums, in order.Rubber Soul: It introduced the sitar to rock, on Norwegian Wood.
The Beatles' UK studio albums, in order.Revolver: Tomorrow Never Knows used looped tapes and backwards sounds.
The Beatles' UK studio albums, in order.Sgt. Pepper's: Its cover features a crowd of famous faces, including Marilyn Monroe and Bob Dylan.
The Beatles' UK studio albums, in order.The White Album: Officially titled The Beatles, its first copies carried individual serial numbers.
The Beatles' UK studio albums, in order.Abbey Road: The cover shows the band on the zebra crossing outside their studio, and it was the last album they recorded.
The Beatles' UK studio albums, in order.Let It Be (album): It came out after the band split but was recorded earlier than Abbey Road, with Phil Spector producing.

Heavier than you'd think.Hummingbird: The bee hummingbird weighs under 2 g, less than a dime, and hummingbird hearts can beat well over 1,000 times a minute in flight.
Heavier than you'd think.Golf ball: Rules cap a golf ball at 1.62 oz; its roughly 300 to 500 dimples cut drag and let it fly much farther than a smooth ball would.
Heavier than you'd think.Human brain: Only about 2% of body weight, the brain burns roughly 20% of the body's energy even at rest.
Heavier than you'd think.Bowling ball (max): The 16-pound limit on ten-pin balls is where this figure comes from; lighter balls exist so that children can play.
Heavier than you'd think.Blue whale's heart: Recorded heart rates in diving blue whales have dropped to about 2 beats per minute, an astonishingly slow pulse for the biggest heart on Earth.
Heavier than you'd think.Concert grand piano: A concert grand is about 2.7 m long, and its iron frame must resist some 20 tonnes of combined string tension.
Heavier than you'd think.Blue whale's tongue: The tongue pushes gulped water back out through the baleen plates, leaving a mouthful of krill trapped inside.
Heavier than you'd think.African elephant: An elephant's trunk holds tens of thousands of muscle units but no bones, which makes it strong enough to uproot a tree yet precise enough to pick up a coin.
Heavier than you'd think.Statue of Liberty: Its copper skin weighs about 30 tonnes yet is only around 2.4 mm thick; the rest of the weight is the iron framework and base.
Heavier than you'd think.Fluffy cumulus cloud: A puffy cloud holds roughly 500 tonnes of water, yet it floats because the droplets are tiny and rising air keeps them aloft.

Cyclones and typhoons that made history.Typhoon Vera: Also called the Isewan Typhoon, it hit Japan's Ise Bay in September 1959 and killed over 5,000 people.
Cyclones and typhoons that made history.Bhola cyclone: The deadliest tropical cyclone on record killed 300,000 or more, and the poor response fed Bangladesh's independence movement.
Cyclones and typhoons that made history.Cyclone Tracy (Darwin): It struck Darwin around Christmas, destroyed most of the buildings and led Australia to tighten its building codes.
Cyclones and typhoons that made history.Typhoon Nina: Its rains helped cause China's Banqiao Dam failure, one of the deadliest dam disasters ever.
Cyclones and typhoons that made history.Typhoon Tip: It remains the largest tropical cyclone ever recorded, roughly 2,200 km across, with the lowest pressure ever measured.
Cyclones and typhoons that made history.Odisha super cyclone: One of the strongest storms in the Bay of Bengal, it killed around 10,000 people in India's Odisha.
Cyclones and typhoons that made history.Cyclone Nargis: It hit Myanmar's Irrawaddy Delta and killed over 130,000, and the ruling junta delayed foreign aid.
Cyclones and typhoons that made history.Typhoon Haiyan: It hit the Philippines with some of the strongest winds at landfall, and about 6,300 people died, mostly around Tacloban.
Cyclones and typhoons that made history.Cyclone Idai: It hit Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Malawi, flooding the port of Beira, among the worst storms in the southern hemisphere.
Cyclones and typhoons that made history.Cyclone Gabrielle: It struck New Zealand's North Island in February 2023, triggering a national state of emergency and heavy flooding.

Body rhythms, by length of one cycle.Gamma brain wave: Gamma waves cycle at around 40 Hz and are associated with focused attention.
Body rhythms, by length of one cycle.Alpha brain wave: Hans Berger detected the roughly 10 Hz alpha rhythm in the 1920s, the first human EEG.
Body rhythms, by length of one cycle.Resting heartbeat: At about 70 beats a minute, a heart will beat roughly 2.5 billion times in a lifetime.
Body rhythms, by length of one cycle.Resting breath: Adults take 12 to 20 breaths a minute, and we can control this rhythm consciously.
Body rhythms, by length of one cycle.Stomach muscle wave: Waves of stomach muscle contraction occur about three times a minute, mixing food.
Body rhythms, by length of one cycle.Sleep cycle: A night consists of four to six of these cycles of light, deep and REM sleep.
Body rhythms, by length of one cycle.Circadian rhythm: It means 'about a day', and a 2017 Nobel Prize went to discoveries about the genes behind it.
Body rhythms, by length of one cycle.Menstrual cycle: It is close to the lunar month in length, but no link to the Moon has been shown.
Body rhythms, by length of one cycle.Seasonal rhythms: Some people experience seasonal affective disorder, a winter low linked to shorter daylight.
Body rhythms, by length of one cycle.Human generation: Only about ten generations cover roughly 250 years of family history, which is why you can trace so few ancestors back to the 1700s.

Viscosity: how thick each fluid is.Hydrogen gas: Unlike liquids, gases get thicker as they are heated, since faster molecules collide more often.
Viscosity: how thick each fluid is.Air: Air is about 55 times less viscous than water, but it is still the main thing a car's engine must fight at highway speed.
Viscosity: how thick each fluid is.Acetone: Because it is thin and evaporates fast, it makes a powerful solvent, which is why nail polish remover is mostly acetone.
Viscosity: how thick each fluid is.Water: Water at room temperature is about 1 mPa·s, a handy benchmark, and hot water is noticeably runnier.
Viscosity: how thick each fluid is.Blood: Blood is thicker than water mostly because of its red cells, and dehydration makes it a little thicker still.
Viscosity: how thick each fluid is.Olive oil: Chilled in a fridge, olive oil thickens and can turn cloudy as parts of it begin to solidify.
Viscosity: how thick each fluid is.Castor oil: This unusually thick plant oil from castor beans was used to lubricate early aircraft engines, because it stayed viscous under heat.
Viscosity: how thick each fluid is.Honey: Warming honey drops its viscosity sharply, which is why it pours easily from a jar left on a warm shelf.
Viscosity: how thick each fluid is.Pitch (tar): In an experiment at the University of Queensland, begun in 1927, fewer than ten drops of pitch have fallen.
Viscosity: how thick each fluid is.Earth's mantle: Solid rock here slowly flows over millions of years, driving plate tectonics, and land still rebounds after the last ice age.

Medieval cities, from north to south.Nidaros (Trondheim): Norway's pilgrimage centre around St Olaf's shrine; its cathedral is often called the northernmost medieval cathedral in the world.
Medieval cities, from north to south.Novgorod: A trading republic ruled partly by a town assembly, the veche; its soil preserved hundreds of birch-bark letters written by ordinary people.
Medieval cities, from north to south.Edinburgh: Built along a volcanic ridge with its castle on top, the medieval Old Town grew unusually tall because there was little room to spread.
Medieval cities, from north to south.London: For centuries London Bridge carried shops and houses across the Thames, and heads of traitors were displayed on spikes at its gatehouse.
Medieval cities, from north to south.Paris: By about 1300 it was probably the largest city in Christian Europe, with roughly 200,000 people, and home to a famed university.
Medieval cities, from north to south.Venice: Built on lagoon islands atop millions of wooden piles, it grew rich on trade, and its Arsenal could assemble galleys at astonishing speed.
Medieval cities, from north to south.Constantinople: Capital of the Byzantine Empire for over a thousand years, guarded by massive land walls until the Ottomans took it in 1453.
Medieval cities, from north to south.Granada: The last Muslim kingdom in Iberia, crowned by the Alhambra palace; it fell to Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492.
Medieval cities, from north to south.Cairo: Founded by the Fatimids in 969, it soon had al-Azhar, still counted among the oldest universities in the world.
Medieval cities, from north to south.Timbuktu: A desert trading hub famed for gold, salt and a rich scholarly tradition; its libraries held manuscripts that survive in private hands today.

When these scientific institutions were.Royal Society: Its motto, 'Nullius in verba', means 'take nobody's word for it', urging members to test claims by experiment.
When these scientific institutions were.French Academy of Sciences: Set up under Louis XIV's minister Colbert, it later played a central role in creating the metric system.
When these scientific institutions were.Royal Observatory, Greenwich: Founded by Charles II to improve navigation by the stars, it stands on the prime meridian, longitude zero, adopted in 1884.
When these scientific institutions were.Royal Institution: It has run the Christmas Lectures since 1825, and Humphry Davy and Michael Faraday did their research here.
When these scientific institutions were.Smithsonian Institution: Founded with money left by James Smithson, an English scientist who never visited the United States.
When these scientific institutions were.Pasteur Institute: Founded after Louis Pasteur's rabies vaccine, it later identified the virus that causes AIDS, in 1983.
When these scientific institutions were.First Nobel Prizes awarded: Funded by dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel's will; the first physics prize went to Wilhelm Röntgen for X-rays.
When these scientific institutions were.World Health Organization: In 1980 it declared smallpox eradicated, the first human disease ever to be wiped out.
When these scientific institutions were.CERN: Near Geneva, it runs the Large Hadron Collider, and Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web while working there.
When these scientific institutions were.NASA: Created the year after the Soviet Sputnik launch, it replaced an older aeronautics committee and ran the Apollo missions.

Metals by melting point.Mercury: The only metal that is liquid at room temperature, once used in thermometers, and highly toxic.
Metals by melting point.Gallium: This silvery metal melts in your hand, and pranksters make spoons from it that vanish into hot tea.
Metals by melting point.Tin: Bending a bar of it makes a crackling sound known as 'tin cry', and mixing it with copper makes bronze.
Metals by melting point.Lead: Its low melting point makes it easy to cast; Romans used it for pipes, and its Latin name plumbum gave us 'plumbing'.
Metals by melting point.Zinc: It is used to galvanise steel, protecting it from rust, and alloyed with copper to make brass.
Metals by melting point.Aluminium: Once costlier than gold, it was used to cap the Washington Monument in 1884, as a showpiece of rare metal.
Metals by melting point.Silver: Sterling silver is 92.5 percent silver, with copper added for strength, since pure silver is too soft for cutlery.
Metals by melting point.Gold: Pure gold is 24 carat, and since it never tarnishes, ancient goldsmiths could work it with simple furnaces.
Metals by melting point.Iron: Humans learned to smelt it during the Iron Age, and Earth's core is mostly made of this metal.
Metals by melting point.Tungsten: It has the highest melting point of any metal, its symbol W comes from 'wolfram', and it makes bulb filaments.

When Western science first described the.Platypus: Early specimens were suspected of being a hoax: a duck-billed, beaver-tailed animal that lays eggs yet is a mammal.
When Western science first described the.Gorilla: It was described by Thomas Savage and Jeffries Wyman, long after travelers' tales of hairy 'wild men' in West Africa.
When Western science first described the.Giant panda: A French missionary, Armand David, brought a skin to Europe; it is one of the best-known bears for its bamboo diet.
When Western science first described the.Okapi: The okapi is the giraffe's closest living relative, and its striped legs look like a zebra's.
When Western science first described the.Komodo dragon: Reports from Dutch colonial officials brought word of this giant lizard, which is the heaviest living lizard.
When Western science first described the.Bonobo: Long mistaken for a small chimpanzee, it was recognized as a separate species and is as close to us as chimps.
When Western science first described the.Coelacanth (found alive): Thought extinct for 66 million years, one turned up in a South African fishing trawler's catch and was recognized by a museum curator.
When Western science first described the.Megamouth shark: The first one was caught when it tangled in a US Navy ship's sea anchor off Hawaii.
When Western science first described the.Saola: Known from skulls found in Vietnam, this 'Asian unicorn' has been seen in the wild only rarely.
When Western science first described the.Olinguito: This cat-sized relative of raccoons was the first new carnivore species described in the Americas in about 35 years.

Far-north cities from north to south.Longyearbyen, Svalbard: The northernmost permanent settlement of any size has a seed vault nearby, and its residents are banned from dying there, since bodies do not decompose.
Far-north cities from north to south.Tromsø: This Norwegian city is a prime spot for viewing the aurora, and the sun does not rise for about two months in winter.
Far-north cities from north to south.Fairbanks: This Alaskan city hosts the ice sculpture festival, and in midsummer its sun hardly sets, while winter days are very short.
Far-north cities from north to south.Yellowknife: The capital of Canada's Northwest Territories sits on Great Slave Lake, and it is known as a prime viewing spot for the northern lights.
Far-north cities from north to south.Anchorage: Alaska's largest city is larger in area than some states and has about 40 percent of the state's people, as well as numerous moose.
Far-north cities from north to south.St Petersburg: Founded by Peter the Great, the Russian city is known for its summer White Nights, when the sky never gets fully dark.
Far-north cities from north to south.Juneau: The Alaskan capital cannot be reached by road, and it is reachable only by plane or boat.
Far-north cities from north to south.Edinburgh: The Scottish capital sits at roughly the same latitude as Moscow yet has a much milder climate thanks to the North Atlantic Drift.
Far-north cities from north to south.Dublin: The Irish capital sits further north than any part of the United States outside Alaska, apart from some of its northernmost cities.
Far-north cities from north to south.London: The British capital lies further north than any other major city in the contiguous US and Canada's southern cities such as Toronto.

Landmark science books, by publication.Copernicus: De revolutionibus: The book by the Polish astronomer put the Sun at the centre of the universe, and the first copy was said to have been given to him on his deathbed.
Landmark science books, by publication.Galileo's Dialogue: This book about the two world systems cost Galileo his freedom, since the Inquisition made him spend his life under house arrest.
Landmark science books, by publication.Newton's Principia: The book laid out the laws of motion and universal gravitation, and it was written in Latin, and it is the foundation of classical mechanics.
Landmark science books, by publication.Linnaeus: Systema Naturae: The Swedish naturalist's book classified nature and began the system of binomial nomenclature, and its first edition was just 11 pages.
Landmark science books, by publication.Lavoisier's Traité: The French chemist's textbook helped found modern chemistry, and it listed the elements, and his wife illustrated it.
Landmark science books, by publication.Lyell: Principles of Geology: The book argued that the Earth was shaped by slow forces still operating today, and it influenced Charles Darwin.
Landmark science books, by publication.On the Origin of Species: Charles Darwin's book introduced natural selection, and the first print run sold out on the first day.
Landmark science books, by publication.Silent Spring: Rachel Carson's book exposed the dangers of pesticides, and it is credited with helping launch the environmental movement.
Landmark science books, by publication.The Selfish Gene: Richard Dawkins coined the term 'meme' in this book, and it popularised the view of genes as the units of evolution.
Landmark science books, by publication.A Brief History of Time: Stephen Hawking's book sold more than 25 million copies, and it was famously written with only one equation.

Composers, by how many numbered symphoni.Sergei Rachmaninoff: He wrote three symphonies, and the first flopped so badly at its premiere that it sent him into a deep depression.
Composers, by how many numbered symphoni.Johannes Brahms: He waited until age 43 to finish his first symphony, intimidated by the long shadow of Beethoven.
Composers, by how many numbered symphoni.Felix Mendelssohn: He wrote five symphonies, including the famous Scottish and Italian, which were inspired by his travels.
Composers, by how many numbered symphoni.Pyotr Tchaikovsky: His sixth, the Pathétique, premiered just days before his death in 1893, and its quiet ending is unusual for a symphony.
Composers, by how many numbered symphoni.Jean Sibelius: He wrote almost nothing major for about three decades before his death, and he reportedly burned his eighth symphony.
Composers, by how many numbered symphoni.Ludwig van Beethoven: His ninth, with the Ode to Joy, was the first major symphony to include voices, and he was deaf by then.
Composers, by how many numbered symphoni.Dmitri Shostakovich: He wrote 15 symphonies, many under Soviet pressure, and his Leningrad symphony was composed during the siege of that city.
Composers, by how many numbered symphoni.Havergal Brian: An English composer who wrote most of his symphonies after age 70, his Gothic Symphony needs a giant orchestra and several choirs.
Composers, by how many numbered symphoni.Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart: He wrote his first symphony at age 8, and the last, Jupiter, is among the greatest ever composed.
Composers, by how many numbered symphoni.Joseph Haydn: Often called the father of the symphony, he wrote more than any other major composer, including a famous one with a surprise loud chord.

Lengths of long (and short) vehicles.Peel P50: The Peel P50 is the smallest production car ever made, with three wheels, one door and no reverse gear.
Lengths of long (and short) vehicles.Smart Fortwo: The Smart Fortwo is short enough to be parked nose-in, perpendicular to the curb, in tight city spots.
Lengths of long (and short) vehicles.Routemaster bus: London's iconic Routemaster, in service from 1956, let passengers hop on and off at the open rear platform.
Lengths of long (and short) vehicles.Articulated city bus: Bendy buses bend in the middle on a flexible joint; London phased out its fleet of them by 2011.
Lengths of long (and short) vehicles.Union Pacific Big Boy: Union Pacific built 25 of these huge steam locomotives in the 1940s, and No. 4014 was restored to running in 2019.
Lengths of long (and short) vehicles.Australian road train (max): Road trains of up to 53.5 m haul cattle and goods across the Australian Outback, pulling several trailers at once.
Lengths of long (and short) vehicles.Saturn V rocket: At 110.6 m, taller than the Statue of Liberty, the Saturn V carried astronauts to the Moon, and all 13 launches succeeded.
Lengths of long (and short) vehicles.Hindenburg airship: Hindenburg was nearly as long as the Titanic, 245 m against 269 m, and the largest aircraft ever flown.
Lengths of long (and short) vehicles.Seawise Giant: The Seawise Giant, a supertanker, was the longest ship ever built; it was sunk in the Iran-Iraq war, refloated and later scrapped.
Lengths of long (and short) vehicles.Record BHP iron-ore train: In 2001 BHP ran an iron-ore train of 682 wagons through Western Australia, the longest and heaviest ever.

When these emoji joined the Unicode stan.Pile of poo: Pile of poo originated in Japanese mobile phone sets, and is now a smiling face used worldwide.
When these emoji joined the Unicode stan.Vulcan salute: Leonard Nimoy invented the gesture for Spock, basing it on a priestly blessing he saw in his Jewish childhood.
When these emoji joined the Unicode stan.Taco: Taco Bell backed a petition for a taco emoji in 2014, and it duly arrived the following year.
When these emoji joined the Unicode stan.Avocado: Botanically, an avocado is a single-seeded berry, and the emoji arrived in 2016 at the height of avocado toast mania.
When these emoji joined the Unicode stan.T-rex: Tyrannosaurus rex means tyrant lizard king, and its bite is estimated to be among the strongest of any land animal ever.
When these emoji joined the Unicode stan.Bagel: Bagels are boiled before baking, which gives them their chewy crust; the emoji arrived in 2018.
When these emoji joined the Unicode stan.Sloth: Sloths move so slowly that algae grows in their fur, and they descend to the ground about once a week to defecate.
When these emoji joined the Unicode stan.Bubble tea: Bubble tea, with its chewy tapioca pearls, was invented in Taiwan in the 1980s and has spread worldwide since.
When these emoji joined the Unicode stan.Melting face: The melting face was added in 2021 and can show embarrassment, feeling overwhelmed, or just being too hot.
When these emoji joined the Unicode stan.Shaking face: Unicode 15 also added a pink heart, a jellyfish and a khanda alongside the shaking face, which seems to vibrate.

Release years of these landmark albums.Sgt. Pepper's (The Beatles): Its cover collages dozens of famous faces around the band, and it is often credited with turning pop albums into unified art statements.
Release years of these landmark albums.The Dark Side of the Moon: It stayed on the US Billboard 200 for more than 900 weeks in total, and its prism cover is among rock's most recognizable images.
Release years of these landmark albums.Rumours (Fleetwood Mac): Written while band members were splitting up with each other, it still became one of the best-selling albums of all time.
Release years of these landmark albums.Thriller (Michael Jackson): With estimated sales around 70 million, it is widely listed as the best-selling album ever, helped by landmark videos like the title track.
The title song sounds like a flag-waver but actually laments how Vietnam veterans were treated; the album produced seven top-10 US singles.
Release years of these landmark albums.Nevermind (Nirvana): It knocked Michael Jackson's Dangerous from the top of the US chart in early 1992, and the cover shows a baby swimming after a dollar bill.
Release years of these landmark albums.OK Computer (Radiohead): Parts were recorded in a grand English country mansion once owned by actress Jane Seymour, and its themes of tech alienation proved prophetic.
Release years of these landmark albums.Back to Black (Amy Winehouse): Produced with Mark Ronson and others, it helped Winehouse win five Grammys in one night in 2008, including Record of the Year for Rehab.
Release years of these landmark albums.21 (Adele): Named after Adele's age while she wrote it, it spent many weeks atop the charts worldwide and sold over 30 million copies.
Release years of these landmark albums.Lemonade (Beyoncé): Released first as a film on HBO, this "visual album" mixes genres from rock to country and drew heavily on Southern Black women's history.

Supercar and luxury car makers, by found.Bugatti: Founded in Molsheim, in Alsace, by Italian-born Ettore Bugatti, whose cars won Grand Prix races in the 1920s.
Supercar and luxury car makers, by found.Aston Martin: The British brand took half its name from Lionel Martin and half from the Aston Hill climb, where he raced.
Supercar and luxury car makers, by found.Maserati: Its trident logo is based on the statue of Neptune in a Bologna fountain, the company's home city.
Supercar and luxury car makers, by found.Bentley: W. O. Bentley's cars won Le Mans in the 1920s, and the "Bentley Boys" who raced them were society celebrities.
Supercar and luxury car makers, by found.Ferrari: The prancing horse emblem came from the family of a World War I Italian flying ace, Francesco Baracca.
Supercar and luxury car makers, by found.Lamborghini: A tractor maker, Ferruccio Lamborghini, decided to build his own sports cars, supposedly after a clash with Enzo Ferrari.
Supercar and luxury car makers, by found.Pagani: Founder Horacio Pagani, an Argentine, once worked at Lamborghini, and his first model, the Zonda, was named after an Andean wind.
Supercar and luxury car makers, by found.Koenigsegg: The Swedish firm's founder, Christian von Koenigsegg, started it in his twenties, and it holds speed records.
Supercar and luxury car makers, by found.Lucid (as Atieva): It started as a startup called Atieva before turning to luxury electric sedans, and the Air model had a very long range.
Supercar and luxury car makers, by found.Rimac: Mate Rimac began building electric cars in his Croatian garage, and his company later took a stake in Bugatti.

US cities by population (city proper).Cheyenne: The Wyoming capital, with a Frontier Days rodeo, is among the smallest US state capitals.
US cities by population (city proper).Anchorage: About 40 percent of Alaska's population lives here, and in midsummer the sun barely sets.
US cities by population (city proper).Miami: It's unusual among major US cities in being founded by a woman: Julia Tuttle.
US cities by population (city proper).Boston: Its Common, created in 1634, is generally called the oldest public park in the US.
US cities by population (city proper).San Francisco: Its cable cars are the only moving national historic landmark.
US cities by population (city proper).Phoenix: Its name comes from the mythical bird that rose from ashes, alluding to the ancient canals of the Hohokam it was built over.
US cities by population (city proper).Houston: The city hosts mission control at the Johnson Space Center, and is where astronauts said 'Houston, we've had a problem'.
US cities by population (city proper).Chicago: After the Great Fire of 1871 it was rebuilt, and in 1900 engineers reversed the flow of its river.
US cities by population (city proper).Los Angeles: The full original name, in Spanish, is El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles.
US cities by population (city proper).New York City: Hundreds of languages are spoken across the five boroughs, making it among the most linguistically diverse cities on Earth.

Harry Potter moments, in story order.Harry learns he's a wizard: Hagrid delivers the news on Harry's 11th birthday: Yer a wizard, Harry.
Harry Potter moments, in story order.Harry kills the basilisk: Harry stabs the basilisk with Gryffindor's sword, and phoenix tears heal him.
Harry Potter moments, in story order.Harry meets Sirius Black: Sirius, wrongly imprisoned in Azkaban, turns out to be Harry's godfather.
Harry Potter moments, in story order.Cedric Diggory dies: Wormtail kills him after the Triwizard Cup becomes a portkey to a graveyard.
Harry Potter moments, in story order.Dumbledore's Army is formed: It forms in secret at the Hog's Head, to resist Umbridge's rule.
Harry Potter moments, in story order.Sirius Black dies: He falls through the veil at the Department of Mysteries, killed by Bellatrix Lestrange.
Harry Potter moments, in story order.Dumbledore dies: Snape kills him on the Astronomy Tower at the end of Half-Blood Prince.
Harry Potter moments, in story order.Ron destroys the locket: Ron destroys Slytherin's locket with Gryffindor's sword after hearing Parseltongue.
Harry Potter moments, in story order.Snape dies: In the Shrieking Shack he gives Harry memories that reveal his lifelong love for Lily.
Harry Potter moments, in story order.Voldemort is defeated: His own Killing Curse rebounds off the Elder Wand, which had become loyal to Harry.

Moons by how long one orbit takes.Mimas (Saturn): Mimas has a huge crater, Herschel, which makes it look like the Death Star, and it orbits Saturn very close.
Moons by how long one orbit takes.Deimos (Mars): Deimos is Mars's smaller moon, and it's tiny, only about 12 km across, and it rises in the east.
Moons by how long one orbit takes.Io (Jupiter): Io is the most volcanically active body in the solar system, and its volcanoes erupt sulfur plumes.
Moons by how long one orbit takes.Europa (Jupiter): Europa has an ocean under its icy shell, and it holds twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans, and it's a target in the search for life.
Moons by how long one orbit takes.Triton (Neptune): Triton orbits Neptune backward, and it's likely a captured Kuiper Belt object, with nitrogen geysers.
Moons by how long one orbit takes.Ganymede (Jupiter): Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system and bigger than Mercury, and it has its own magnetic field.
Moons by how long one orbit takes.Titan (Saturn): Titan has thick orange atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane, and Huygens landed on it in 2005.
Moons by how long one orbit takes.Hyperion (Saturn): Hyperion tumbles chaotically and looks like a sponge, and its odd shape comes from its cratered surface.
Moons by how long one orbit takes.Iapetus (Saturn): Iapetus is two-toned, with one side dark and the other bright, and it has a ridge around its equator.
Moons by how long one orbit takes.Nereid (Neptune): Nereid has one of the most eccentric orbits of any moon, and it probably is a captured body.

Sherlock Holmes stories, by publication.A Study in Scarlet: Holmes's debut, where he first meets Dr Watson. Conan Doyle reportedly sold the rights for a flat £25.
Sherlock Holmes stories, by publication.The Sign of the Four: The second novel opens with Holmes using cocaine, and builds to a Thames boat chase over a stolen Agra treasure.
Sherlock Holmes stories, by publication.A Scandal in Bohemia: The first short story, and the one introducing Irene Adler, the one woman who outwitted Holmes and earned his lasting respect.
Sherlock Holmes stories, by publication.The Adventures (collection): Twelve stories from The Strand Magazine made Holmes a sensation. They include The Red-Headed League and The Speckled Band.
Sherlock Holmes stories, by publication.The Final Problem: Conan Doyle, tired of his hero, sent Holmes over the Reichenbach Falls with Moriarty. Outraged readers reportedly cancelled their subscriptions.
Sherlock Holmes stories, by publication.The Hound of the Baskervilles: Set on foggy Dartmoor with a spectral dog, it revived Holmes in print, though it was written as a case from before his supposed death.
Sherlock Holmes stories, by publication.The Return (collection): Opens with The Empty House, where Holmes returns after three years and explains he faked his death at Reichenbach.
Sherlock Holmes stories, by publication.The Valley of Fear: The fourth and last Holmes novel. Its second half flashes back to a violent secret society in Pennsylvania coal country.
Sherlock Holmes stories, by publication.His Last Bow: Subtitled 'An Epilogue of Sherlock Holmes', its title story finds the retired detective posing as a spy on the eve of World War I.
Sherlock Holmes stories, by publication.The Case-Book (collection): The final collection of twelve stories includes The Creeping Man, and two of them are narrated by Holmes himself, not Watson.

The Hundred Years' War, in order.War begins: Edward III claimed the French crown after a dispute over Gascony. The conflict actually lasted 116 years, and the name was coined much later.
The Hundred Years' War, in order.Battle of Crécy: English archers with longbows slaughtered French knights here. It's one of the first big battles to show the power of the longbow.
The Hundred Years' War, in order.Battle of Poitiers: The Black Prince captured the French king, John II, here. The enormous ransom for him strained France for years.
The Hundred Years' War, in order.Treaty of Brétigny: This treaty gave England about a third of France and a huge ransom for the king. It didn't last, and fighting resumed within a decade.
The Hundred Years' War, in order.Battle of Agincourt: Henry V's tired, outnumbered men beat the French on a muddy field. Shakespeare gave it the "Band of Brothers" speech.
The Hundred Years' War, in order.Treaty of Troyes: The treaty named Henry V as heir to the French throne and married him to Catherine of Valois. It disinherited her brother, the dauphin.
The Hundred Years' War, in order.Siege of Orléans lifted: A teenage Joan of Arc helped end this siege in about nine days. It turned the tide for France.
The Hundred Years' War, in order.Joan of Arc burned: Joan was tried for heresy and burned at the stake in Rouen. She was only about 19, and was declared a saint in 1920.
The Hundred Years' War, in order.Battle of Formigny: French cannons crushed an English army here, ending English power in Normandy. The French then took the rest of the region in months.
The Hundred Years' War, in order.Battle of Castillon: The French used massed artillery to win, and the English commander, Talbot, died. It's usually seen as the last battle of the war.

Physics' oddball length units.Planck length: The smallest meaningful length, where quantum gravity matters; it is about twenty orders of magnitude smaller than a proton.
Physics' oddball length units.Fermi: Named for Enrico Fermi; one proton is about one of these across, and physicists often call it a femtometer.
Physics' oddball length units.Bohr radius: The distance of the electron from the nucleus in the simplest model of hydrogen, which Niels Bohr proposed in 1913.
Physics' oddball length units.Ångström: Named for Anders Ångström; a hydrogen atom is about one across, so it suits measuring atoms and light wavelengths.
Physics' oddball length units.Light-nanosecond: Grace Hopper handed out 30 cm lengths of wire as 'nanoseconds' to show how far light goes in that time.
Physics' oddball length units.Cubit: Based on the forearm, and ancient Egypt's royal cubit was about 52 cm, used in building pyramids.
Physics' oddball length units.Smoot: Oliver Smoot went on to become chairman of the American National Standards Institute, and later president of ISO.
Physics' oddball length units.Light-second: The Moon is about 1.3 of these away, and the Sun is around 500, which is why sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us.
Physics' oddball length units.Astronomical unit: Redefined in 2012 as exactly 149,597,870,700 m, it is the average Earth-Sun distance, and astronomers use it in the solar system.
Physics' oddball length units.Parsec: Short for 'parallax second', it is the distance at which a star shifts by one arcsecond as Earth orbits the Sun.

Taylor Swift's albums, in order.1989: Named for her birth year, it was her first fully pop album and won Album of the Year in 2016.
Taylor Swift's albums, in order.Taylor Swift (debut): Taylor Swift wrote songs as a teenager in Nashville, and her debut gave her the youngest sole songwriter credit on a major country label.
Taylor Swift's albums, in order.Fearless: The album won Album of the Year at the 2010 Grammys, with hits like Love Story and You Belong with Me.
Taylor Swift's albums, in order.Speak Now: She wrote every song herself, a point she made clear after critics doubted teen pop stars' songwriting.
Taylor Swift's albums, in order.Red: The album leans into pop while keeping stories like the ten-minute All Too Well, later re-recorded.
Taylor Swift's albums, in order.Reputation: Responding to years of tabloid attacks, the album used snake imagery and the hit Look What You Made Me Do.
Taylor Swift's albums, in order.Lover: Her first release after leaving Big Machine Records, it began her push to own her master recordings.
Taylor Swift's albums, in order.Folklore: Surprise-released in July 2020, during the pandemic, it was created with Aaron Dessner and won Album of the Year at the Grammys.
Taylor Swift's albums, in order.Midnights: Released in October 2022, it let her occupy all ten top spots of the Billboard Hot 100 at once.
Taylor Swift's albums, in order.The Tortured Poets Department: The album arrived in April 2024 and became a 31-song double release, with a streaming opening on a record-breaking scale.

Making cheese, step by step.Warm the milk: Cheese was possibly discovered when milk carried in an animal-stomach bag curdled, so the story goes.
Making cheese, step by step.Add starter culture: Bacteria in the culture turn lactose into lactic acid, giving flavor and starting the curdling.
Making cheese, step by step.Add rennet: The enzyme chymosin traditionally comes from calf stomachs, but microbial rennet is now widely used.
Making cheese, step by step.Cut the curd: Smaller curds expel more whey, so the cutting size helps decide whether a cheese is soft or hard.
Making cheese, step by step.Cook and stir the curds: Heating shrinks the curds and expels whey; hard cheeses like Parmesan are cooked at higher temperatures.
Making cheese, step by step.Drain the whey: A kilo of cheese typically leaves about nine litres of whey, which gets turned into ricotta.
Making cheese, step by step.Press into molds: Some cheeses like Camembert skip pressing and drain under their own weight.
Making cheese, step by step.Salt or brine: Salt draws out whey, slows spoilage bacteria, and helps form the rind; Parmesan soaks in brine for weeks.
Making cheese, step by step.Age: Parmigiano-Reggiano must age at least 12 months, and many are aged two years or more.
Making cheese, step by step.Slice and serve: Take it out of the fridge an hour before; cold mutes its flavor.
